title: Bhadda Kapilani
hookLine: Kassapa's wife parts from him at a crossroads, later becomes a nun, and is named foremost among the nuns in remembering past lives (AN 1.14; Therigatha)

lines: RIGHT FOR HIM, LEFT FOR HER.
cards: He takes the road to the right. She takes the road to the left. That's the whole parting, as the commentary tells it.
Pippali and Bhadda, who married as friends and left home together, had been walking one behind the other in simple robes since they left their great house. At a crossroads they stop.
People who see them pass might think they're still a couple, and that could cloud the life they've chosen. So at the fork they go separate ways. We followed him for most of a week.

teach.b: First, the parting. In the commentary it's done with respect, not regret. They've shared a house and a friendship; now each walks toward the same goal by a separate road.

teach.h: SHE WAITED FOR AN ORDER OF NUNS.
teach.b: When Bhadda left, the commentary says, there was not yet an order of nuns. So she waited, and lived the homeless life as best she could.
Later, when women were ordained, she was ordained among them, and in time she reached the goal. Third, her gift.

In the list of foremost disciples, the Buddha names Bhadda Kapilani foremost among the nuns who remember past lives. Not because of her husband: in her own right, in her own line of the list. Fourth, her own verses.

In the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, Bhadda begins by praising Kassapa: the Buddha's true heir, who knows his former lives and has reached the end. Then she turns and says the same of herself.
She too has that knowledge; she too has come to the end. They both saw the misery of the world, she says, and went forth, and both are now freed, at peace.
She doesn't make herself smaller to praise him, or him smaller to claim her place.
She stands beside him in the poem the way she walked beside him out of the house.
Then she walks her own road.

how: Theravada Buddhists honor Bhadda Kapilani among the great nuns of the Buddha's time, and her verses are read with the other elder nuns' poems in the Therigatha.

o: a queen who gave the monks a park
a nun foremost in remembering past lives
the Buddha's foster mother, the first nun

p: he goes right, she goes left
until there was an order of nuns
where her own verses are kept

s: Bhadda is remembered only as Kassapa's wife
she is named foremost among the nuns who remember past lives, and she has her own verses.
in the commentary he took the road to the right and she the road to the left.
her verses praise Kassapa and say nothing of herself
she praises him, then says the same knowledge and freedom are hers too.

games.q: you're Bhadda, walking behind the man you left home with. people might mistake you for a couple still. what do you do?
o: part at the crossroads and take your own road.
games.why: at the crossroads he goes right and she goes left; later she is ordained and reaches the goal in her own right.

practice: Bring to mind someone you're close to, a spouse, a partner, a sibling, a best friend, and a road they walk that isn't yours: a faith, a calling, a craft, a grief. Don't try to join it or fix it.
Just picture them on that road, wish them well on it, and stay with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Bhadda Kapilani. Kassapa's wife, who parted from him at a crossroads, became a nun, and is named foremost among the nuns who remember past lives. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pubbenivasa, former lives: remembering them is the gift for which Bhadda is named foremost among the nuns.

carryVoice: Your line: her own path. Side by side, and still her own. Until tomorrow.
